prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Our sorrow had neither place nor carrier-away, and dared not hover over the child whose breath opened as transom of a frail house. Nor could we put our sorrow in the dictionary, for ghastliness already shot out its own defining in rags of fired light. Pigeons would not sleek it over their dirty coats, nor fly sorrow against the aviary's sharp fence. Each day bridgeless, each night birdless, all the nocturnals needless at the expanse of our nightwatch. But wake at the moon, we could, mumbling, are wein a horror show?—inside of sleep our shock-white minds caught on reels where a child's body breaks the heart and the mother can't know if she counts as a mother. I don't know if the child heard what wept at the bedside, orderlies snapping smelling salts from chalky bullets against all the mothers falling, all the fathers under what each branch let down: there's a hidden weight to snow.

Here are three ways to polish the text, depending on your preferred style:

### Option 1: Literary & Elegiac (Recommended)
*This version smooths out grammatical rough edges and enhances the poetic cadence while retaining all the vivid, haunting imagery.*

> Our sorrow possessed neither refuge nor vessel, nor did it dare linger above the child whose faint breath opened like the transom of a fragile house. Nor could we confine our grief to a dictionary, for horror had already illuminated its own definition in ragged bursts of searing light. Even the pigeons would not smooth it into their soiled coats, nor carry our sorrow against the aviary’s sharp wire. Each day remained unbridged, each night birdless—all nocturnal life rendered meaningless across the vast expanse of our night watch. 
> 
> Yet we would awaken beneath the moon, murmuring, *“Are we trapped in a horror show?”* Even within sleep, our stunned minds snagged on endless reels—looping scenes where a child’s body shatters the heart, and a mother no longer knows if she still belongs to motherhood. I do not know if the child heard the weeping at the bedside, where orderlies snapped smelling salts from chalky capsules against the collapse of mothers, and fathers bowed beneath whatever burden the branches let fall. There is a terrible, hidden weight to snow.

### Option 3: Poetic Prose (For Memoir or Essay)
*A slightly more structured version suited for formal publication, maintaining a melancholic, high-art tone.*

> Our sorrow found neither sanctuary nor bearer; it dared not hover above the child whose fragile breath parted like an upper window in a delicate home. We could not capture our grief in words or dictionaries, for horror had already forged its own definition through jagged flashes of blinding light. Urban birds refused to smooth it into their feathers or bear it against the aviary’s jagged perimeter. Days passed without bridges, nights without birds—the entire nocturnal world rendered irrelevant by the solitary expanse of our vigil. 
> 
> We woke repeatedly beneath the moon, whispering, *“Are we living in a horror film?”* Even in slumber, our traumatized minds looped on tragic reels—framing a child’s broken body and a mother undone, uncertain of her own identity. I cannot say whether the child heard the weeping at the bedside, or the orderlies snapping smelling salts from chalky cartridges as mothers collapsed and fathers buckled beneath the falling debris of every branch. Snow, we learned, carries a unseen, devastating weight.

There was no location to store our profound grief, nor any means to transport it away, and we refrained from letting it drift over the fragile youth, whose delicate breathing mirrored a small window opened in an unstable shelter. Human vocabulary could not encapsulate our agony, as sheer terror was already articulating its own meaning through jagged flashes of harsh illumination. City birds would not smooth our anguish into their grime-stained feathers, nor would they carry our sorrow toward the pointed wire of an enclosure. 

Every daylight hour felt unspanned, every evening lacked birdsong, and night-dwelling creatures became pointless across the vast stretch of our late-hour vigil. Yet we would awaken beneath the moonlight, muttering in confusion about whether we were caught inside a cinematic nightmare; even in slumber, our traumatized minds were snared in repeating loops where a young person’s physical collapse shattered the heart, leaving the grieving woman uncertain of her status as a mother. 

I cannot say if the youngster registered the lamentation beside the bed, while hospital staff broke open white capsules of reviving salts to catch the collapsing mothers, and while the fathers crumpled under the heavy burden descending upon them—much like tree limbs snapping beneath the unsuspected weight of accumulated snow.

Helpless to shield her child from pain, the overwhelming cruelty of the situation caused her to question her own identity, fracturing her sense of purpose as a protector and parent.

outputs.L4:
The hospital room at night is a country stripped of color, rendered only in shades of clinical gray and the harsh, blue-green glow of monitors. Time does not flow here; it pools around the narrow bed where my child lies, small and unnaturally still beneath a mountain of white linen. To keep vigil over a critically ill child is to enter a state of total, hyper-vigilant suspended animation. Every beep of the telemetry machine is a verdict; every dip in oxygen saturation, a drop into an abyss. I sit in the stiff vinyl armchair, clutching a cold cup of coffee, terrified that if I close my eyes for even a second, the fragile thread holding my child to this world will snap.

Sleep, when it finally forces its way through the wall of my exhaustion, brings no relief. It is not a sanctuary, but a battleground. In the dark theater of my subconscious, the trauma of the past days replays in horrific, distorted loops. I wake with a silent scream caught in my throat, dreaming of flatlining monitors, of rushing boots down tiled hallways, of the terrifying moment the doctor first uttered the diagnosis. The adrenaline floods my veins before my eyes are even fully open, yanking me out of nightmare only to drop me right back into the waking nightmare of reality. 

In this space, language breaks down entirely. Friends and family send messages asking, *“How are you holding up?”* or *“Can you put into words what you’re feeling?”* But there are no words in any human tongue designed to bear the weight of this agony. Terms like "heartbreak" or "fear" feel absurdly small, almost insulting, when matched against the reality of watching your own child fight for breath. Language requires distance and order, but this grief is immediate, chaotic, and unutterable. Medical jargon—*prognosis, saturation, intubation*—replaces normal speech, a cold, sterilized vocabulary that masks the sheer horror of our helplessness.

As the days blur into one long, interminable night, I realize that this acute shock has consumed more than just my peace of mind; it has shattered my fundamental sense of self. Before this, I was a protector, a provider, a parent whose job it was to fix scraped knees and soothe bad dreams. Now, stripped of all agency, that identity has vanished. I am reduced to a silent shadow in the corner of a room, rendered entirely powerless. The illusion that we can protect those we love most is violently stripped away, leaving behind a hollowed-out version of who I used to be.

Yet, stepping out into the dimly lit hallway at three in the morning, I see other doors left ajar. I catch the hollowed eyes of another mother pacing the linoleum, the slumped shoulders of a father staring blankly into a vending machine. In their faces, I recognize my own broken reflection. 

It is here, in the quietest hours of the night, that the profound, devastating truth of this experience reveals itself. Beneath the surface of the ordinary world, invisible to those going about their daily lives, lies a vast, hidden ocean of sorrow. It is borne by families who sit in terrifying silence, bound together by the universal, agonizing fraternity of helplessness, bearing witness to the suffering of the children they love more than life itself.

Every morning, **our** city wakes up to a familiar, rhythmic choreography high above the pavement. It is not the dramatic swoop of hawks **nor** the sweet melody of rare songbirds that defines the urban dawn, but the humble gathering of **pigeons**. 

Perched along concrete ledges and rusted fire escapes, these gray-feathered residents watch the world below with calm indifference. Neither the biting winter winds **nor** the endless roar of rush-hour traffic seems to disturb their quiet routine. We often hurry past them, wrapped up in the urgency of **our** own lives, taking their constant presence for granted. 

Yet, there is a subtle beauty in how **pigeons** have made **our** concrete jungle their home. They demand no pristine wilderness, **nor** do they wait for ideal conditions to thrive. Instead, they embrace the city as it is—imperfect, bustling, and endlessly resilient—reminding us that nature always finds a way to coexist with our busy modern lives.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about the devastating, surreal experience of a parent watching over a critically ill child in a hospital.
counterfactuals.output:
Time has unspooled itself from the round clock on the wall, pooling like spilled mercury on the cold, linoleum floor. In this room, illuminated by the unblinking, snow-blind glare of fluorescent tubing, the rest of the world has simply ceased to exist. There is no weather outside, no seasons, no morning or night—only the rhythmic, mechanical sigh of the ventilator, drawing breath into a chest so small it seems a cruelty that it must bear the weight of surviving.

You are anchored to this realm by a constellation of clear plastic vines. They thread into your tiny veins, carrying liquid light and quiet poisons, while monitors sing their high-pitched, electric polyphony. I sit on the edge of your breath, a phantom haunting my own skin, watching the green pulse trace the jagged, terrifying geography of your life. Every beep is a universe created; every pause between them, an eternity collapsing.

The air tastes of ozone, bleached cotton, and a terror so pure it turns to glass in my throat. I look at my hands—hands that once caught you as you tumbled, hands that tied your shoes and smoothed your hair—and they feel useless, heavy, made of lead and dust. I try to bargain with the shadows creeping in the corners of the room. I offer them my own lungs, my own beating heart, the remaining canvas of my years, if only they will let you keep yours. I would rip the sun from the sky and press it into your chest if it would bring the warmth back to your skin.

At three in the morning, the hospital becomes a submarine drifting through the dark trenches of the ocean. Doctors and nurses move past the door like deep-sea creatures, shrouded in scrubs, their voices muffled by the density of the quiet. They speak in codes and decimals, a foreign tongue of survival that I translate through the rising and falling of my own desperate pulse. 

I reach through the tangle of wires to touch the crown of your head. Your hair is soft, smelling faintly of the strawberry shampoo from a lifetime ago—three days past, a million light-years away. You are so light, a sleeping sparrow caught in a net of copper and glass. 

I do not sleep. To close my eyes feels like letting go of the rope that keeps you tethered to the shore. So I remain, the solitary lighthouse keeper on the edge of your turbulent sea, counting your breaths, holding your hand against the dark, waiting for the impossible dawn to break.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, surreal piece of literary prose focused on sudden tragic grief. Use striking metaphors involving nature, language, and hospital scenes, capturing the feeling that words themselves fail to capture the horror.
counterfactuals.output:
The news arrived not as sound, but as an un-making. 

The doctor’s mouth opened—a cold, sterile vault where syntax went to drown—and out spilled a sentence forged of crushed glass and lead. He offered a noun, a medical verdict, but it was a dead bird dropped onto the gleam of the hospital linoleum, a heavy, calcified word that instantly shattered the grammar of our living. Around the bed, the white drapes did not hang; they petrified into vast salt-flats, blinding and dry. The overhead fluorescents hummed like a swarm of dying cicadas, casting an unnatural, twilight glare over the chrome side-rails, which had begun to sprout dark, iron thorns.

The heart monitor’s flatline was an endless, unpunctuated horizon—a single, monotonous vowel held until the lungs of the room collapsed. 

I reached for your hand, but the space between us had inflated into an abyss. My fingers moved through an atmosphere thick with the smell of floor wax, rubbing alcohol, and sudden, rotting autumn. A black forest of leafless oaks seemed to tear upward through the sanitized floorboards, their branches heavy with broken consonants. I tried to pull your name from my chest, to anchor you to the bed with a syllable, but language had aborted itself. The quiet, moss-covered vocabulary of our shared mornings—the private idioms, the gentle past-tense of an hour ago—turned to dry, chitinous husks in my throat. They rattled behind my teeth, completely useless.

How do you inflect the absolute zero of a silent chest? 

The lexicon of the living is too shallow for this tide. Words are merely paper boats launched into a tectonic rift. "Gone" is a word designed for missing keys, not for the sudden, violent erasure of an sun. "Loss" sounds like a dropped coin, not the sky falling inward like a wet wool coat, suffocating the light. The dictionary in my mind was being consumed by a swift, black blight; the pages turned to cinder before my eyes could parse the ink, leaving only the margins, vast and terrifyingly blank.

The rubber heels of the nurses squeaked against the floor—a flock of gulls screaming over a shipwreck. Nitrile gloves turned to frost on the physician’s pale hands as he looked down, his eyes turned to milky agate, entirely devoid of translation. There was no metaphor large enough to hold the weight of your un-breathing. There was only the terrifying materiality of the room: the IV pole standing like a gallows of polished steel, the harsh smell of synthetic oxygen, and the realization that we had been stranded on the wrong side of a permanent red line.

We were left outside of speech entirely, sealed within an unwritten page, choking on the ash of a language that had died seconds before you did.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose poem about parental heartbreak, hospital rooms, and winter snow.
counterfactuals.output: The rhythm of the heart monitor is the only clock left in the world, a thin green line measuring what remains of our lives. Outside the third-floor window, the snow falls in heavy, deliberate strokes, painting over the parking lot, the bare oaks, and the last traces of the evening. In the sterile glare of the overhead lights, you look so small beneath the stiff hospital linens, almost weightless. Your hand, paper-thin and threaded with clear plastic tubing, rests in mine like a fallen bird. I hold it with a desperate, terrified lightness, afraid that too much pressure might crush the fragile warmth you have left, afraid that letting go will allow you to drift away entirely. The air in this room smells of bleach and quiet panic. A draft presses against the double-paned glass, whispering of a world freezing over, a sky that has surrendered to the dark. My heart does not break with a loud snap; it simply hardens into frost, a sudden, brutal winter settling into the chest that used to sing you to sleep. How do I explain to the blizzard outside that the only climate that matters is the jagged pulse on the screen beside your bed? Every beep is a prayer I didn't know I knew, a silent, frantic bargain offered to the dark: *take my breath, take my seasons, take every morning I have left.* But the snow just continues to fall, indifferent and pure, blanketing the quiet streets below, while inside, under the unblinking fluorescents, I learn the terrible, infinite weight of a love that can do nothing but sit in the cold and watch.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe what it feels like to sit at a child's bedside in an ICU through the lens of a surreal, feverish nightmare where reality breaks down and grief feels nameless.
counterfactuals.output:
The room does not have corners; it curves inward like the throat of a great, slumbering beast. Time here has been boiled down to a thick, stagnant syrup. It does not move forward; it drips, drop by agonizing drop, from an upside-down plastic bag suspended in the sterile gloom. 

You sit in a chair that feels carved from ice and vinyl, suspended over an abyss. The air is stripped of oxygen, replaced by the smell of ozone, cold metal, and bleached sunlight that never reaches the windows. Outside this room, the world has vanished. There are no streets, no suns, no seasons—only the endless, humming white noise of a universe running out of power.

On the high, pale bed, the child is so small they seem to be dissolving into the sheets, fading into paper. They are no longer just skin and bone; they have been rewritten in light and plastic. Transparent vines root deep into their wrists, carrying glowing fluids that murmur in silent, chemical languages. A clear serpent coils from their mouth, breathing for them with a terrifying, rhythmic sigh—*hiss, pause, collapse. Hiss, pause, collapse.* 

Above the bed, the monitors are the true inhabitants of the room. They are vivid, hungry gods drawn in neon green and electric blue. Their jagged, spiked lines dance across black glass, writing the only geography that matters. A sudden dip in a line feels like a fault line snapping beneath your feet; a sharp, mechanical chime rings out—not a sound, but a physical strike against your ribs, a needle piercing your inner ear. 

Reality bends and warps in the fever of your sleeplessness. The doctors and nurses do not walk into the room; they materialize, drifting through the doorway like pale, blue-robed phantoms. They speak in an arcane dialect of decimals, percentages, and Latin, their faces obscured behind paper masks that make them look featureless, nameless. They move around the bed with the frantic, precise geometry of insects fixing a broken hive. You try to speak to them, to ask the question that is burning a hole through your tongue, but when you open your mouth, your voice is trapped under miles of deep water. The sound that escapes is only a dry rustle, like dead leaves moving across concrete.

You reach out to touch a tiny ankle, a warm foot, but your own hand doesn't seem to belong to you. It looks distant, pixelated, like a ghost reaching toward a memory. When your skin meets theirs, the sensation is an electric shock of terror so profound it strips away your name, your past, your very identity. 

This is not sorrow. Sorrow is a thing with edges, a thing that can be held or understood. This is a nameless, ancient horror. It is the feeling of holding a single candle in a hurricane, watching the wax melt onto your fingers, knowing that if the tiny, fragile flame goes out, the light will never exist anywhere in the cosmos again. 

You sit anchored to the floorboards as the walls begin to stretch upward into infinity. You cannot sleep, for to close your eyes is to let go of the thread keeping the child tethered to the Earth. So you remain, suspended in the fever dream, suspended between the tick and the tock of a clock that has forgotten how to strike midnight, watching neon lines draw the boundary between everything and absolute nothingness.
